title: Firsthand and Secondhand Accounts
keyIdea: A firsthand account is written or told by someone who was there, such as a diary, a letter, an autobiography or an eyewitness interview. A secondhand account is written by someone who was not there and pieced it together from records, interviews and other sources, such as a biography, a textbook or an encyclopedia. Accounts of the same event differ in focus: the firsthand one zooms in on what one person saw, heard and felt, using I and we, while the secondhand one zooms out to numbers, causes and what happened later, in calm, neutral words. Neither is simply better; each answers different questions, so good readers compare both.
familyTip: Next time something happens at home, like a power cut or a big storm, each write three sentences: one of you as I was there, one as a reporter writing about it a week later. Swap and spot the clues: who used I, who gave numbers, who told how it felt?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: was the writer there? Compare a diary and a history book about one flood.

kid: A firsthand account is told by someone who was there. A diary, a letter or your own life story is firsthand. The writer often says I or we.

A secondhand account is told by someone who was not there. They found out from books, records or other people. A biography or a textbook is secondhand. A biography is about one person, but someone else wrote it.
The two kinds tell different things. Firsthand shows what one person saw, heard and felt. Secondhand gives the big picture, like numbers, causes and what happened next.
One is not better. Pick the one that answers your question. Read both to get the whole story.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. The US Common Core asks Grade 4 readers to compare a firsthand and a secondhand account of the same event (RI.4.6). They describe how the two differ in focus and in the facts each gives. In England, Year 5 and 6 readers tell fact from opinion and make comparisons across books, which uses the same skill.

The test is one question: was the writer there? Diaries, letters, logbooks, autobiographies and eyewitness interviews pass it. Biographies, textbooks and encyclopedias do not. Then look at focus: one person close up, or the whole event. Look at the facts: senses and feelings, or numbers, causes and results. Look at the words: I and we, or they and people.

Common mistakes: calling a biography firsthand because it is about one person; thinking an autobiography is secondhand because it covers a whole life; believing one kind is always more true; and treating any line with I as firsthand without asking if the writer was really there.

In the lab your child sorts ten sources, then eight lines from two accounts of one flood: a girl's diary and a history book. They place nine details in a Venn diagram and match eight questions to the account that can answer them. Then they rewrite four diary lines in a history-book voice.

choices: a letter from a girl at the Olympics
a book about the history of the Olympics
an encyclopedia page on the Olympics
practice.explain: The girl was at the Olympics, so her letter is firsthand. The book and the encyclopedia were written by people who found out later.

practice.prompt: A class reads {n} sources about a storm. {f} were written by people who were there. How many are secondhand?
practice.hint: Take away the ones written by people who were there.
practice.explain: {n} − {f} = {=n-f} sources were written by people who found out later, so they are secondhand.

practice.prompt: Which question can only a firsthand account answer?
choices: What did the smoke smell like?
How many homes burned?
What year was it?
practice.hint: Which one needs someone who was there?
practice.explain: Only someone who was there knows how the smoke smelled. A secondhand account can give the number of homes and the year from records.

practice.prompt: Sam compares {a} diary entries with {b} textbook pages about the same event. How many texts does he read in all?
practice.hint: Add the diary entries and the textbook pages.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} texts. Reading both kinds gives him the close-up view and the big picture.

practice.prompt: A biography of a famous scientist is…
choices: secondhand, because someone else wrote it
firsthand, because it is about her life
firsthand, because it has facts
practice.hint: Who wrote it, and were they there?
practice.explain: A biography is written by someone else, so it is secondhand. Being about one person does not make it firsthand.

choices: firsthand
secondhand
neither
pool.hint: Auto means self. Who writes it?
pool.explain: In an autobiography the writer tells their own life, so they were there: firsthand.

pool.prompt: Which line most likely comes from a secondhand account?
choices: Records show 2,000 people left the city.
I held my brother's hand as we ran.
We could hear the sirens all night.
pool.hint: Look for numbers and records, not I or we.
pool.explain: A count from records is the kind of fact a later writer gathers. The other two lines tell what the writer saw and did.

pool.prompt: A diary and a textbook describe the same flood. How are they different?
choices: The diary zooms in on one person; the textbook gives the big picture.
The diary has no facts at all.
The textbook tells how it felt.
pool.hint: Think about focus: one person or the whole town?
pool.explain: The diary shows one person close up, with feelings and small details. The textbook zooms out to numbers, causes and results.

pool.prompt: You want to know why a bridge fell down. Which account helps most?
choices: a report written after experts checked it
a diary by someone who crossed it that day
a postcard with a photo of the bridge
pool.hint: Causes are found out later by people who check.
pool.explain: The cause was found by experts after the event, so the secondhand report answers why. The diary tells what it was like that day.

pool.prompt: A Venn diagram has {d} details only in the diary, {b} in both and {t} only in the textbook. How many details are in the textbook account?
pool.hint: The textbook circle holds the middle part and its own part.
pool.explain: {b} + {t} = {=b+t}. The details in both are in the textbook too, so count the overlap.

pool.prompt: Which words are typical of a firsthand account?
choices: I, we, my and feeling words
historians, records and dates
they, people and numbers
pool.hint: Who is telling it: someone who was there, or not?
pool.explain: Someone who was there writes I, we and my, and often says how it felt. The others are typical of a later writer.

pool.prompt: Ravi says a firsthand account is always true. What is the best reply?
choices: It shows one person's view, which can miss things.
Yes, the writer was there.
No, it is always made up.
pool.explain: Being there gives close-up detail, but one person sees only part of the event. Compare it with other accounts.

pool.prompt: A website has {s} sources. {e} are eyewitness letters and the rest are later reports. How many later reports are there?
pool.explain: {s} − {e} = {=s-e} later reports, written by people who were not there: secondhand.

pool.prompt: How would a history book most likely write the diary line 'We were soaked and shivering'?
choices: Many families were left wet and cold.
We were so cold!
Nobody got wet.
pool.hint: A later writer uses they or people and calm words.
pool.explain: The history book uses people or families and calm words. We were so cold still sounds like someone who was there, and Nobody got wet changes the facts.

pool.prompt: Which is a secondhand account of a football final?
choices: a magazine article written from interviews a year later
the captain's own diary of the match
a fan's text message from the stadium
pool.hint: Which writer was not at the match?
pool.explain: The magazine writer pieced it together later, so it is secondhand. The captain and the fan were there.
